900100.title: The Sprint Solve Format
900100.description: One puzzle, one clock, one winner: the anatomy of a sprint.
900100.content:
The Sprint Solve Format — One puzzle, one clock, one winner: the anatomy of a sprint.

The sprint is the purest race in puzzling: every solver gets the identical puzzle and the clock decides. The format works because it isolates solving skill from puzzle choice — no one can blame the draw. The classic sprint is the crossword dash: fifteen minutes, one grid, the fastest clean solve wins, with penalties for wrong squares. The organizer's duties are few but absolute: identical puzzles, synchronized starts, and a judging standard published before the first pencil moves. The sprint's drama is compression — an hour of thinking collapsed into minutes of visible racing. Run one and watch quiet solvers become athletes.

Key points:
- Identical puzzles for every solver.
- Synchronized starts; published judging rules.
- Penalties for errors keep speed honest.
- Compression is the drama.

900101.title: Relay Races: Team Puzzle Sprints
900101.description: Four solvers, one baton, zero slack: the relay done right.
900101.content:
Relay Races: Team Puzzle Sprints — Four solvers, one baton, zero slack: the relay done right.

The puzzle relay turns solitary solving into a team sport: each leg hands a solved state to the next solver, and the baton is a checked answer. The design key is leg independence — every leg must be solvable from a clean handoff, so a weak leg never dooms the team beyond its own minutes. The classic structure is four legs of escalating difficulty, with the anchor leg deliberately the hardest so the finish stays uncertain. The handoff ritual matters: the incoming solver reads the answer aloud, the judge confirms, the next solver starts fresh. The relay's lesson: teams win on trust in the handoff, not just speed in the legs.

Key points:
- Legs must be independent and cleanly handed off.
- Escalate difficulty toward the anchor leg.
- Judged handoffs keep the race honest.
- Trust in the handoff wins relays.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - Relay Races: Team Puzzle Sprints

900102.title: The Marathon Solve
900102.description: Twelve hours, one giant puzzle, and the long game of stamina.
900102.content:
The Marathon Solve — Twelve hours, one giant puzzle, and the long game of stamina.

The marathon solve is puzzling's endurance event: a single enormous puzzle — a 5,000-piece jigsaw, a mega-crossword, a multi-stage hunt — attacked over a full day. The skill being tested is not speed but pacing: solvers who sprint the first hour fade by the fourth, while steady solvers own the back half. The organizer's craft is logistics: food, light, seating, and a scoring system that rewards partial progress so nobody quits at hour six. The marathon's psychology is the wall — every solver hits one, and the ones who plan breaks push through. The finish line feeling is earned precisely because the middle was miserable.

Key points:
- Pacing beats sprinting over twelve hours.
- Logistics are the organizer's real craft.
- Score partial progress to prevent quitting.
- Plan breaks; the wall is inevitable.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Marathon Solve

900103.title: Head-to-Head Brackets
900103.description: Single elimination for puzzlers: the bracket as theater.
900103.content:
Head-to-Head Brackets — Single elimination for puzzlers: the bracket as theater.

The bracket takes sixteen solvers and crowns one champion through head-to-head heats, and its genius is narrative: every round is a story with a winner and a loser. The format demands fast puzzles — five-minute sprints work; hour-long epics don't, because the audience and the schedule can't wait. The seeding question is real: random draws create Cinderella runs, ranked seeds protect the favorites, and the crowd loves both for different reasons. The bracket's cruelty is the single loss — the best solver can die in round one on a bad puzzle. The consolation bracket fixes this: nobody travels to lose once. Run the bracket as theater and the puzzle becomes a spectator sport.

Key points:
- Fast puzzles only: five-minute heats.
- Seeding shapes the tournament's story.
- Add a consolation bracket for fairness.
- The bracket is theater; stage it.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - Head-to-Head Brackets

900104.title: The Handicap System: Racing Fairly
900104.description: How experts and beginners race the same puzzle honestly.
900104.content:
The Handicap System: Racing Fairly — How experts and beginners race the same puzzle honestly.

The handicap is what lets a grandmaster and a newcomer race the same puzzle without the outcome being a foregone conclusion. The simplest fair system is staggered starts: the expert begins minutes late, calibrated from past results, so both finish near each other at full effort. The subtler system is puzzle-tiering: same race, different puzzle difficulties, with par times that equalize. The handicap's data problem is calibration — it takes three or four races to set honest numbers, and sandbagging poisons the well. The culture fix is transparency: publish everyone's handicap and the formula, and cheaters lose the room's trust. Done right, the handicap turns a coronation into a contest.

Key points:
- Staggered starts equalize mixed fields.
- Calibrate from three or four past races.
- Publish handicaps and the formula.
- Transparency defeats sandbagging.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Handicap System: Racing Fairly

900105.title: Puzzle Hunt Leg Races
900105.description: Checkpoint to checkpoint: the city as a racetrack.
900105.content:
Puzzle Hunt Leg Races — Checkpoint to checkpoint: the city as a racetrack.

The leg race sends teams across a city or campus, solving at checkpoints to earn the next location. The design tension is travel versus thinking: too much travel and it's a footrace, too much thinking and teams bunch up at hard puzzles. The craft is the clue chain — each solved puzzle reveals the next checkpoint, and the reveal should feel earned, not arbitrary. The safety rules are non-negotiable: defined bounds, daylight hours, check-in intervals, and a staffed base. The leg race's magic is the city transformed: familiar streets become a game board for a day. The winning team is usually the one that navigates best, not the one that solves fastest.

Key points:
- Balance travel against thinking time.
- Clue chains must feel earned.
- Safety rules are non-negotiable.
- Navigation skill decides leg races.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - Puzzle Hunt Leg Races

900106.title: The Blind Solve Challenge
900106.description: No peeking, no notes: solving from memory alone.
900106.content:
The Blind Solve Challenge — No peeking, no notes: solving from memory alone.

The blind solve strips puzzling to its essence: the solver studies the puzzle, then solves it without looking — from memory, on a blank sheet. The discipline comes from cubing, where blindfolded solves are a competitive event with memorization as a separate timed phase. The training path is staged: first memorize small puzzles, then solve with periodic peeks, then commit to full blind. The failure mode is always the same — memory decays under pressure, and the solver must learn to encode robustly, not just quickly. The blind solve's payoff is a different relationship with the puzzle: you stop seeing pieces and start seeing structure. The eyes were a crutch; the mind was the solver all along.

Key points:
- Memorization is a separately timed skill.
- Train in stages: small, then peeked, then blind.
- Encode robustly, not just quickly.
- Blind solving reveals structure.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Blind Solve Challenge

900107.title: Race Directing: Running a Fair Contest
900107.description: The invisible craft behind every clean competition.
900107.content:
Race Directing: Running a Fair Contest — The invisible craft behind every clean competition.

The race director is the most important person nobody watches: they set the rules, hire the judges, and absorb the complaints so the solvers can solve. The director's bible is the rulebook — written before the race, covering ties, disputes, equipment failure, and cheating, because improvising rules mid-race destroys trust. The director's hardest moment is the disputed finish: the protocol is stop the clock, sequester the evidence, rule from the book, and move on. The director's secret weapon is the dry run: staff solve the puzzles, test the timing, and break the plan before race day. The clean race feels effortless; the effort is all the director's.

Key points:
- Write the rulebook before race day.
- Disputes follow protocol, not improvisation.
- Dry-run everything with staff.
- Clean races are directed, not lucky.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - Race Directing: Running a Fair Contest

900108.title: The Photo-Finish: Judging Close Calls
900108.description: When two solvers finish a breath apart: the judging craft.
900108.content:
The Photo-Finish: Judging Close Calls — When two solvers finish a breath apart: the judging craft.

The photo-finish is the race's crucible: two solvers claim the win and the evidence is thin. The prevention is instrumentation — synchronized clocks, filmed finishes, and answer sheets timestamped by judges, not solvers. The ruling principle is published tiebreakers: fewest errors beats fastest time, or a sudden-death playoff puzzle decides it, but the rule must exist before the race. The judge's demeanor matters as much as the ruling: calm, quick, and final, because lingering disputes poison the room. The photo-finish's lesson for directors: you don't rise to the occasion, you fall to the level of your preparation. Build the system before you need it.

Key points:
- Instrument finishes: clocks, film, timestamps.
- Publish tiebreakers before the race.
- Judges rule calmly, quickly, finally.
- Preparation beats improvisation.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Photo-Finish: Judging Close Calls

900109.title: The Victory Lap: Race Traditions
900109.description: Trophies, rituals, and the culture that keeps racers returning.
900109.content:
The Victory Lap: Race Traditions — Trophies, rituals, and the culture that keeps racers returning.

The victory lap is everything after the winner is declared: the trophy, the speech, the photo, the story told for years. The traditions are what convert a contest into a community — the traveling trophy with engraved winners, the loser's toast, the annual rematch. The smart organizer designs traditions deliberately: a distinctive prize, a ceremony with gravity, and a record book that makes every edition part of a lineage. The victory lap's economics are simple: people return for belonging, not prizes. The race ends; the tradition compounds. Build the rituals and the racers will build the legacy.

Key points:
- Traditions convert contests into community.
- Design the ceremony deliberately.
- Keep a record book: every edition is lineage.
- Belonging brings racers back.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Victory Lap: Race Traditions

900110.title: The Dovetail Secret Drawer
900110.description: A drawer that isn't there: the dovetail's hidden geometry.
900110.content:
The Dovetail Secret Drawer — A drawer that isn't there: the dovetail's hidden geometry.

The secret drawer is the puzzle box's signature move: a compartment invisible in the finished piece, revealed only by a sequence of slides and tilts. The dovetail joint is the mechanism's backbone — its angled tails lock under load but slide free in exactly one direction, which is the secret's physics. The build sequence matters: cut the carcass first, fit the drawer to the void, then close the case so the seams vanish. The tolerance is the whole game: a tenth of a millimeter too tight and the drawer jams forever; too loose and the secret rattles. The finished box should survive a skeptic's shake. The drawer isn't hidden by magic — it's hidden by precision.

Key points:
- Dovetails lock in all but one direction.
- Fit the drawer before closing the case.
- Tolerances decide secrecy: tight but free.
- The box must survive a skeptic's shake.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Dovetail Secret Drawer

900111.title: The Cryptex Cylinder
900111.description: Five rings, one word, and the letter-lock's beautiful logic.
900111.content:
The Cryptex Cylinder — Five rings, one word, and the letter-lock's beautiful logic.

The cryptex is the puzzle box's most theatrical form: rotating rings of letters that align to a password, releasing the end cap. The mechanism is a stack of disks with a gated channel — only the correct alignment opens the path for the locking pin. The build is a lathe project: turn the core, cut the ring grooves, engrave the letters, and fit the pin with a spring that forgives nothing. The password choice is the maker's signature: pick a word with personal meaning, because the solver will remember the word longer than the mechanism. The cryptex's drama is the final click — five rings snap into line and the cylinder surrenders. Theater, engineered.

Key points:
- Gated channels make the letter-lock work.
- Lathe work: core, grooves, letters, pin.
- Choose a memorable password word.
- The final click is the payoff.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Cryptex Cylinder

900112.title: Hidden Compartments 101
900112.description: The grammar of secrecy: every hidden space obeys rules.
900112.content:
Hidden Compartments 101 — The grammar of secrecy: every hidden space obeys rules.

Every hidden compartment, from the simplest sliding panel to the nested Russian-doll box, obeys the same grammar: the void must be planned before the case is closed, the access must be a deliberate sequence, and the reveal must be discoverable without destruction. The beginner's mistake is building the box first and hunting for hiding places after — the void is architecture, not decoration. The classic training progression runs sliding lid, then magnetic catch, then false bottom, then the full secret drawer. The test of every compartment is the drop test of trust: hand it to a friend with no instructions and see if the secret survives an honest shake. Secrecy is a discipline with a curriculum.

Key points:
- Plan the void before closing the case.
- Progress: sliding lid to false bottom to drawer.
- The shake test proves the secret.
- Secrecy is a teachable discipline.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - Hidden Compartments 101

900113.title: The Trick Lock Lid
900113.description: A lid that opens only for those who know the sequence.
900113.content:
The Trick Lock Lid — A lid that opens only for those who know the sequence.

The trick lock lid looks like a plain box top and behaves like a combination lock with no visible dial: press, slide, tilt in the right order and it lifts; force it and it holds. The mechanism is usually a set of internal bolts thrown by a sliding key plate — the sequence moves the plate through gates that only align in one order. The maker's challenge is feedback: the solver needs subtle clicks and shifts to know they're on the path, without the box giving away the answer. The build is fiddly work with small parts and strong opinions about glue. The trick lid's joy is the first opening — the moment the plain box becomes a puzzle. Simple outside; sequenced inside.

Key points:
- Internal bolts thrown by a sequenced plate.
- Give subtle feedback, not answers.
- Small parts demand patience and dry-fits.
- The first opening is the reward.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Trick Lock Lid

900114.title: Puzzle Box Woods: Choosing Timber
900114.description: The material is the mechanism: why wood choice decides everything.
900114.content:
Puzzle Box Woods: Choosing Timber — The material is the mechanism: why wood choice decides everything.

The puzzle box lives or dies by its timber: the wood must be stable, fine-grained, and honest about its movement, because a secret drawer that swells shut in summer is a failure. The traditional choices are the dense hardwoods — walnut, maple, cherry — quarter-sawn for stability and seasoned for years, not months. The contrasting woods are the maker's palette: a dark inlay line can hide a seam, or betray it, depending on the maker's intent. The finishing truth is that oil and wax are structural: they slow moisture exchange and keep tolerances true. The wood is not the box's clothing — in a puzzle box, the wood is the mechanism.

Key points:
- Dense, quarter-sawn, well-seasoned hardwoods.
- Contrast hides seams — or reveals them.
- Oil and wax are structural, not cosmetic.
- The wood is the mechanism.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - Puzzle Box Woods: Choosing Timber

900115.title: The Magnetic Key Box
900115.description: Invisible locks: hiding the key in the magnetic field.
900115.content:
The Magnetic Key Box — Invisible locks: hiding the key in the magnetic field.

The magnetic key box replaces visible locks with hidden magnets: a steel pin inside the box answers only to a magnet held at the right spot outside. The mechanism is a spring-loaded bolt with a ferrous catch — the external magnet lifts the catch against the spring, and the panel slides free. The craft is magnet placement: embed rare-earth magnets in a wooden wand or a decorative knob, and map the invisible target with trial fittings. The failure mode is the stray magnet — a fridge magnet in the wrong pocket can spring your secret at the worst moment. The magnetic box's elegance is its blank face: no keyhole, no seam, no clue. The lock is a field, not a thing.

Key points:
- Spring bolt with a ferrous catch.
- Map the target with trial fittings.
- Beware stray magnets springing secrets.
- A blank face is the deepest disguise.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Magnetic Key Box

900116.title: The Sequential Discovery Box
900116.description: Seven moves in order: the choreography of opening.
900116.content:
The Sequential Discovery Box — Seven moves in order: the choreography of opening.

The sequential discovery box turns opening into choreography: seven moves in exact order — slide, rotate, press, tilt, slide again — each enabling the next. The design principle is dependency: move three physically cannot happen until move two completes, so the solver can't skip ahead by force. The build is a layered mechanism, each layer's gate cut so the previous layer's pin must retract first. The documentation problem is real: the maker must record the sequence, because even the maker forgets a seven-move dance. The sequential box's pleasure is procedural — the solver learns a ritual, and the box opens like a remembered spell. Order is the lock.

Key points:
- Each move must physically enable the next.
- Layer gates so skipping is impossible.
- Record the sequence: makers forget too.
- Order itself is the lock.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Sequential Discovery Box

900117.title: Finishing: Oils, Wax, and Patience
900117.description: The final ten percent that makes the box a heirloom.
900117.content:
Finishing: Oils, Wax, and Patience — The final ten percent that makes the box a heirloom.

The finish is the last ten percent of the work and the first thing anyone touches: oil to feed the wood, wax to seal it, and patience to let each coat cure. The technique is thin coats and long waits — flood the surface and you'll trap dust and fingerprints for a decade. The puzzle-box-specific rule is to finish the moving parts differently: wax the sliding surfaces, oil the show faces, and never varnish a secret drawer shut. The testing ritual is the hand test: close your eyes and feel for catches, drags, and whispers of movement. The finish doesn't just beautify the box — it tunes it. The heirloom feel is friction, managed.

Key points:
- Thin coats, long cures, no floods.
- Wax the slides; oil the show faces.
- The hand test finds what eyes miss.
- Finish tunes the mechanism.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - Finishing: Oils, Wax, and Patience

900118.title: The Gift Box That Fights Back
900118.description: A present with a personality: the playful adversarial box.
900118.content:
The Gift Box That Fights Back — A present with a personality: the playful adversarial box.

The gift box that fights back is a present with a personality: it resists, misdirects, and teases before it surrenders the gift inside. The design rule is playful, never cruel — the box should make the recipient laugh, not cry, so every dead end resolves within minutes and the final opening feels triumphant. The classic gags are the false bottom that opens onto another puzzle, the lid that needs a full rotation, and the note that says 'warmer' or 'colder.' The maker's calibration target is the recipient's skill: build for the person, not for the portfolio. The gift inside matters less than the story of getting it. The box is the present; the contents are the excuse.

Key points:
- Playful, never cruel: dead ends resolve fast.
- Build for the recipient's skill.
- Every gag should earn a laugh.
- The box is the present.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Gift Box That Fights Back

900119.title: The Workshop Bench Setup
900119.description: The bench behind the boxes: tools, jigs, and workflow.
900119.content:
The Workshop Bench Setup — The bench behind the boxes: tools, jigs, and workflow.

The puzzle box bench is a small shop with strong opinions: a reliable square, sharp chisels, a small plane, and jigs for every repeated cut, because puzzle boxes are repetition with tolerances. The workflow runs in batches — cut all the parts, fit all the joints, then assemble — since switching between cutting and fitting wastes the day. The measuring doctrine is cut to the line, then sneak up on the fit: you can always remove wood, never add it. The shop's most valuable tool is the test box: a quick ugly prototype that proves the mechanism before the good wood is risked. The bench is where patience is manufactured. The boxes are just the evidence.

Key points:
- Jigs for every repeated cut.
- Batch the work: cut, fit, assemble.
- Sneak up on fits; never force.
- Prototype ugly before cutting good wood.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Workshop Bench Setup

900120.title: The Ambiguous Cube
900120.description: One drawing, two cubes: the Necker cube's flip.
900120.content:
The Ambiguous Cube — One drawing, two cubes: the Necker cube's flip.

The Necker cube is twelve lines that refuse to sit still: stare at it and the cube flips between two orientations, front face forward or back, with no change in the ink. The flip is the visual system revealing its machinery — the brain must choose a depth interpretation, and when the evidence is perfectly balanced it alternates. The puzzle use is attention training: solvers learn to hold one interpretation deliberately, then release it, which is a learnable skill. The deeper lesson is epistemic: if twelve lines can sustain two true readings, what else in life flips? The cube is a twelve-line philosophy course.

Key points:
- Twelve lines, two stable readings.
- The flip reveals the brain's depth machinery.
- Holding an interpretation is trainable.
- Ambiguity is a feature, not a bug.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Ambiguous Cube

900121.title: The Retina's Ghost Gallery
900121.description: Stare, blink, and see the ghost: the afterimage puzzle.
900121.content:
The Retina's Ghost Gallery — Stare, blink, and see the ghost: the afterimage puzzle.

The afterimage puzzle uses the retina as a canvas: stare at a bright pattern for thirty seconds, then look at a blank wall and watch the ghost appear in complementary colors. The physiology is adaptation — the color receptors fatigue, and the rested opponent channels dominate the blank field. The puzzle design is flag-making: stare at a red-and-green flag, see its ghost in cyan-and-magenta, and the solver experiences color theory as a hallucination. The safety note is real: keep staring times short and brightness moderate. The afterimage's lesson is that seeing is active — the eye is not a camera, it's a chemical instrument with memory.

Key points:
- Thirty seconds of staring paints the ghost.
- Complementary colors emerge from fatigue.
- Keep staring brief and brightness moderate.
- Seeing is active, not photographic.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Retina's Ghost Gallery

900122.title: The Café Wall Illusion
900122.description: Straight lines that lean: the tilted mortar mystery.
900122.content:
The Café Wall Illusion — Straight lines that lean: the tilted mortar mystery.

The café wall illusion shows rows of dark tiles with offset light mortar, and the rows appear to tilt — though every row is perfectly horizontal. The mechanism is contrast and orientation detectors in the visual cortex being fooled by the mortar's zigzag energy. The puzzle value is measurement: solvers who fetch a ruler experience the shock of the straight edge against the lying eye. The design lesson for illusion-makers is that the effect needs the offset — aligned mortar kills it, which is itself a puzzle about necessary conditions. The café wall teaches humility: the eye is a brilliant instrument that can be hacked by grout. Trust, but verify — with a ruler.

Key points:
- Rows are horizontal; the eye says otherwise.
- Offset mortar is the necessary condition.
- The ruler delivers the shock of truth.
- Perception needs verification.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Café Wall Illusion

900123.title: Stereograms: Seeing Depth in Noise
900123.description: Cross your eyes and the flat page goes 3D.
900123.content:
Stereograms: Seeing Depth in Noise — Cross your eyes and the flat page goes 3D.

The stereogram hides a three-dimensional shape inside a flat field of noise, visible only when the eyes converge in front of or behind the page. The technique is the wall-eye or cross-eye method: relax the gaze as if looking through the page until the repeating pattern locks into depth. The puzzle is patience — most people fail for ten minutes and then the shark leaps out of the static forever. The design craft is the depth map: the hidden shape is encoded as horizontal shifts in the pattern, so the maker paints with disparity. The stereogram's reward is a private miracle: a dimension that exists only in the viewer's visual cortex. The page was flat; the seeing wasn't.

Key points:
- Converge the eyes through the page.
- Patience: the shape appears suddenly.
- Makers paint with horizontal disparity.
- Depth lives in the visual cortex.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - Stereograms: Seeing Depth in Noise

900124.title: The Impossible Triangle
900124.description: Three bars, zero logic: the Penrose triangle's paradox.
900124.content:
The Impossible Triangle — Three bars, zero logic: the Penrose triangle's paradox.

The impossible triangle is three bars joined in a loop that the eye accepts and geometry forbids — each corner looks correct locally while the whole cannot exist. The trick is inconsistent depth cues: the drawing feeds the visual system three plausible local readings that never reconcile. The puzzle history runs from Reutersvärd's 1934 cubes through the Penroses' 1958 triangle to Escher's waterfalls, each generation pushing the paradox further. The maker's craft is the local-global split: draw each joint perfectly, and let the contradiction live in the assembly. The triangle's lesson is about local truth: every part can be right while the whole is impossible. Check the assembly, not just the joints.

Key points:
- Locally plausible, globally impossible.
- Depth cues contradict across the joints.
- Draw each joint perfectly; hide paradox in assembly.
- Local truth doesn't guarantee global truth.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Impossible Triangle

900125.title: Motion Illusions: The Spinning Snakes
900125.description: Nothing moves, everything spins: the peripheral drift illusion.
900125.content:
Motion Illusions: The Spinning Snakes — Nothing moves, everything spins: the peripheral drift illusion.

The rotating snakes are a static image that swirls in the peripheral vision — stare directly and it freezes, glance aside and it flows. The mechanism is still debated, but high-contrast repeating patterns with specific color sequences drive motion detectors that normally report real movement. The puzzle use is the freeze test: solvers learn that direct foveal vision and peripheral vision are different instruments with different lies. The design variables are color order, contrast, and repetition — tweak them and the snakes speed up, slow down, or die. The illusion's philosophical kick: motion is not in the world, it's in the processing. The page never moved. You did.

Key points:
- Peripheral vision sees motion that isn't there.
- Direct gaze freezes the illusion.
- Color sequence and contrast tune the effect.
- Motion is computed, not received.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - Motion Illusions: The Spinning Snakes

900126.title: The Hollow Mask
900126.description: A concave face that looks convex: the brain's face priority.
900126.content:
The Hollow Mask — A concave face that looks convex: the brain's face priority.

The hollow mask is the back of a face mask that the brain insists on seeing as a normal protruding face — even when you know it's hollow. The mechanism is the brain's face prior: faces are so important that the visual system overrides depth evidence to keep them convex. The puzzle is the light test: shine light from below and the hollow mask shows impossible shadows, yet the face persists. The demonstration value is enormous — it's the fastest proof that perception is hypothesis, not measurement. The mask's lesson is about priors: the brain would rather be wrong about geometry than wrong about faces. Knowing is not seeing.

Key points:
- The brain overrides depth for faces.
- Impossible shadows don't break the illusion.
- Perception is hypothesis, not measurement.
- Priors can defeat knowledge.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Hollow Mask

900127.title: Color Constancy Puzzles
900127.description: The dress that broke the internet: color is contextual.
900127.content:
Color Constancy Puzzles — The dress that broke the internet: color is contextual.

Color constancy puzzles exploit the visual system's white-balance: the same pixels read as blue-black or white-gold depending on the brain's assumption about the illumination. The famous dress worked because the lighting cues were ambiguous — the brain had to guess the light source, and different brains guessed differently. The puzzle design is illumination ambiguity: strip the context that anchors white balance, and watch consensus collapse. The teaching payoff is the end of naive color realism — color is not a property of objects but a negotiation between light, surface, and brain. The dress was never about the dress. It was about the light you assumed.

Key points:
- Ambiguous illumination splits color perception.
- The brain white-balances every scene.
- Strip context to break consensus.
- Color is a negotiation, not a property.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - Color Constancy Puzzles

900128.title: The Grid That Lies: Hermann's Illusion
900128.description: Ghost spots at every intersection: the Hermann grid.
900128.content:
The Grid That Lies: Hermann's Illusion — Ghost spots at every intersection: the Hermann grid.

The Hermann grid is white lines on black squares, and at every intersection a ghostly gray spot appears — look directly at it and it vanishes. The classic explanation is lateral inhibition in the retina: intersection regions get more surround inhibition, reading as darker. The puzzle is the counting game: try to count the spots and they flee the fovea, an exercise in the limits of attention. The scintillating variant adds flashing dots that amplify the effect into a disco of ghosts. The grid's lesson is architectural: the retina preprocesses before the brain ever sees, and the preprocessing has bugs. The spots were never there. The wiring was.

Key points:
- Ghost spots haunt every intersection.
- Lateral inhibition explains the ghosts.
- Direct gaze banishes them.
- The retina preprocesses — with bugs.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Grid That Lies: Hermann's Illusion

900129.title: Designing Your Own Illusion
900129.description: From observer to maker: the illusionist's toolkit.
900129.content:
Designing Your Own Illusion — From observer to maker: the illusionist's toolkit.

Designing an illusion reverses the puzzle: instead of being fooled, you engineer the fooling, which requires knowing exactly which visual subsystem to target. The toolkit is the catalog of mechanisms — lateral inhibition for grids, opponent channels for afterimages, motion detectors for drift, priors for faces — each with known trigger conditions. The design loop is hypothesis, prototype, test on fresh eyes: the maker is always the worst judge, because knowing the trick kills it. The documentation rule is to record the parameters that work, since illusions are finicky and small changes murder the effect. The maker's reward is the gasp — the moment someone's visual system betrays them on schedule. Fool the eye; enlighten the mind.

Key points:
- Target a specific visual subsystem.
- Test on fresh eyes; makers can't judge.
- Record working parameters precisely.
- The gasp is the maker's reward.

900130.title: Rung One: The Welcoming Puzzle
900130.description: The first rung must say yes: designing the perfect opener.
900130.content:
Rung One: The Welcoming Puzzle — The first rung must say yes: designing the perfect opener.

Rung one is the most important puzzle in the ladder: it must be solvable in minutes by a complete beginner, and it must teach the core mechanic without a lecture. The design pattern is the guided discovery — the puzzle's structure makes the first move obvious, and the obvious move teaches the rule. The failure mode is the false easy: a puzzle the designer finds trivial but beginners find opaque, usually because the designer forgot what not-knowing feels like. The test is the cold open: hand it to someone with zero context and watch. Rung one's job is not to challenge — it's to recruit. Every expert was once someone who solved rung one and thought: I can do this.

Key points:
- Solvable in minutes by a beginner.
- Teach the mechanic without a lecture.
- Test with a true cold open.
- Rung one recruits; it doesn't challenge.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - Rung One: The Welcoming Puzzle

900131.title: Rung Three: The First Real Fight
900131.description: Where the ladder gets honest: the first genuine challenge.
900131.content:
Rung Three: The First Real Fight — Where the ladder gets honest: the first genuine challenge.

Rung three is where the ladder stops being polite: the solver knows the mechanics now, and the puzzle demands they actually use them. The design shift is from tutorial to application — the same rules, but the solution requires planning two or three moves deep. The emotional target is the earned win: hard enough to feel like an achievement, fair enough that the solver blames themselves, not the puzzle, for failures. The calibration tool is the struggle curve: watch solvers and aim for furrowed brows, not thrown pencils. Rung three is the filter that keeps the ladder honest — everyone past this point chose to climb. The fight is the point.

Key points:
- Same rules, deeper application.
- Target furrowed brows, not thrown pencils.
- The win must feel earned.
- Rung three filters for commitment.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - Rung Three: The First Real Fight

900132.title: Rung Five: The Plateau
900132.description: The middle of the ladder: where most climbers stall.
900132.content:
Rung Five: The Plateau — The middle of the ladder: where most climbers stall.

Rung five is the plateau: the solver is competent, the puzzles are genuinely hard, and progress slows to a crawl. The design challenge is motivation management — the puzzles must stay interesting through the long middle, where novelty fades and grind begins. The technique is variety within mastery: new twists on known mechanics, so the solver's hard-won skill keeps paying off in fresh ways. The danger is the difficulty spike disguised as a plateau — a sudden jump that reads as unfair and empties the ladder. The plateau's truth is that it's a feature: the slow middle is where deep skill forms. The climbers who persist past rung five are the ladder's real graduates.

Key points:
- Manage motivation through the long middle.
- Variety within mastery sustains interest.
- No hidden spikes: the plateau must be fair.
- Slow progress builds deep skill.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - Rung Five: The Plateau

900133.title: Rung Seven: The Expert's Crucible
900133.description: For the committed: puzzles that demand everything.
900133.content:
Rung Seven: The Expert's Crucible — For the committed: puzzles that demand everything.

Rung seven is the expert's crucible: the training wheels are off, the mechanics combine in ways the earlier rungs only hinted at, and the solutions require sustained, multi-stage reasoning. The design principle is synthesis — rung seven puzzles don't introduce new rules, they demand new combinations of old ones. The audience is self-selected: only solvers who climbed six rungs arrive here, so the designer can assume fluency and punish shallow thinking. The fairness bar is highest here: an unfair rung-seven puzzle doesn't just frustrate, it insults the investment of the climb. The crucible's reward is mastery made visible — the solver sees, in their own solution, how far they've come. The view from seven is the ladder's gift.

Key points:
- Synthesis, not new rules.
- Assume fluency; punish shallow thinking.
- Fairness matters most at the top.
- Mastery made visible is the reward.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - Rung Seven: The Expert's Crucible

900134.title: Rung Ten: The Legendary Tier
900134.description: The summit: a puzzle worthy of the whole climb.
900134.content:
Rung Ten: The Legendary Tier — The summit: a puzzle worthy of the whole climb.

Rung ten is the legendary tier: a single puzzle that justifies the nine rungs beneath it, solvable only by a solver the ladder itself created. The design is the capstone — every mechanic from the climb returns, combined in a structure that would have been unthinkable at rung one. The practical constraints are real: it must be solvable (test it with your best solvers), it must be fair (no leaps of faith), and it should be beautiful (the summit deserves a view). The completion rate will be tiny and that's correct — rung ten is not for everyone, it's for the legend of the ladder. The solver who finishes stands alone for a while. That's the point of a summit.

Key points:
- The capstone uses every mechanic.
- Test with your best solvers.
- Tiny completion rates are correct.
- The summit is the legend.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - Rung Ten: The Legendary Tier

900135.title: Calibrating Difficulty: The Playtest Loop
900135.description: Difficulty is measured, not guessed: the playtest protocol.
900135.content:
Calibrating Difficulty: The Playtest Loop — Difficulty is measured, not guessed: the playtest protocol.

Difficulty calibration is an empirical discipline: you don't guess how hard a puzzle is, you measure it with playtesters. The protocol is simple: recruit testers at the target skill level, time their solves silently, and record where they stall — the stall points are the puzzle's true difficulty map. The sample size rule is five: five testers reveal the pattern; one tester reveals the tester. The iteration loop is adjust, retest, adjust: soften the stall points that are unfair, keep the ones that are instructive. The calibration's enemy is the designer's curse — you cannot playtest your own puzzle, because you know the answer. The loop's output is a number you can trust. Measure, don't guess.

Key points:
- Time silent playtesters; map the stalls.
- Five testers reveal the pattern.
- Soften unfair stalls; keep instructive ones.
- Never playtest your own puzzle.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - Calibrating Difficulty: The Playtest Loop

900136.title: The Hint Gradient
900136.description: Help without spoiling: the art of the graduated hint.
900136.content:
The Hint Gradient — Help without spoiling: the art of the graduated hint.

The hint gradient is the ladder's safety net: a sequence of hints from nudge to near-spoiler that rescues stuck solvers without robbing them. The design is the reveal curve — hint one reframes the problem, hint two points at the key insight, hint three practically solves it, and the solver chooses how far to descend. The delivery matters: hints should be opt-in and one at a time, because an unasked spoiler is a small theft. The analytics are gold: which hints get taken reveals the puzzle's true difficulty better than solve times. The gradient's philosophy is that a solved-with-hints puzzle beats an abandoned puzzle every time. Help is part of the design.

Key points:
- Graduate hints from nudge to near-spoiler.
- Hints are opt-in, one at a time.
- Hint-taken data maps true difficulty.
- Helped solves beat abandoned puzzles.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Hint Gradient

900137.title: When Easy Is Hard: Perceived Difficulty
900137.description: The puzzle feels impossible but isn't: managing perception.
900137.content:
When Easy Is Hard: Perceived Difficulty — The puzzle feels impossible but isn't: managing perception.

Perceived difficulty is the gap between how hard a puzzle feels and how hard it is — and it decides whether solvers persist or quit. The drivers are presentation: a cluttered layout feels harder than a clean one with identical logic, and an unfamiliar format feels harder than a familiar one with identical depth. The designer's tools are framing: a friendly title, a worked example, and visible progress all lower perceived difficulty without touching the actual puzzle. The danger is the mismatch in the other direction — a puzzle that looks easy but isn't breeds betrayal. The calibration target is honesty: the puzzle should feel exactly as hard as it is. Perception is part of the puzzle.

Key points:
- Presentation drives perceived difficulty.
- Framing tools: titles, examples, progress.
- Never look easier than you are.
- Honest difficulty feels fair.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - When Easy Is Hard: Perceived Difficulty

900138.title: The Ladder Teaches
900138.description: Ten rungs, one education: the ladder teaches.
900138.content:
The Ladder Teaches — Ten rungs, one education: the ladder teaches.

The difficulty ladder is secretly a curriculum: each rung teaches a skill the next rung assumes, and the whole structure is a course in the puzzle's deep logic. The curriculum design runs backwards — decide what rung ten demands, then derive the prerequisites rung by rung down to one. The assessment is built in: a solver who stalls at rung four has a diagnosable gap, and the ladder itself is the diagnostic. The graduation criterion is transfer: the rung-ten solver should handle novel puzzles in the same family, not just the ladder's own. The curriculum's elegance is that nobody signed up for school — they signed up for puzzles, and got an education smuggled inside. The ladder teaches by climbing.

Key points:
- Design backwards from rung ten.
- Stalls diagnose skill gaps.
- Graduation means transfer to novel puzzles.
- Education smuggled inside play.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Ladder Teaches

900139.title: The Capstone: Building a Ten-Rung Set
900139.description: From blank page to full ladder: the complete build.
900139.content:
The Capstone: Building a Ten-Rung Set — From blank page to full ladder: the complete build.

Building a ten-rung ladder is a project with phases: survey the mechanic's space, sketch the summit, derive the prerequisites, draft all ten rungs, playtest each with fresh solvers, and tune until the climb feels inevitable. The project management is the hard part — rungs interact, so a change at rung three ripples upward, and the wise builder locks the lower rungs early. The quality bar is the smooth climb: a tester should never feel a cliff between rungs, only a steady steepening. The launch is the ladder's first real test: watch the first hundred climbers and let their stall points rewrite your calibration. The capstone's truth is that the ladder is never finished — it's tuned, forever, by the climbers. Build it, then listen.

Key points:
- Phases: survey, summit, derive, draft, test, tune.
- Lock lower rungs early.
- No cliffs between rungs: steady steepening.
- Let climbers' data retune the ladder.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Capstone: Building a Ten-Rung Set

900140.title: The Sealed Study
900140.description: A classic impossible crime: the room locked from inside.
900140.content:
The Sealed Study — A classic impossible crime: the room locked from inside.

The sealed study is the locked room's archetype: the victim alone, the door bolted from within, the window latched, and no way in or out — yet the impossible happened. The puzzle's engine is the exhaustive elimination: the solver must account for every entrance, every mechanism, every second. The classic solutions form a catalog — the bolt tricked by thread, the key turned from outside, the window that was never truly latched. The writer's discipline is fair play: the solution's mechanism must be visible in the clues, never smuggled in at the reveal. The sealed study endures because it's a pure logic engine wearing a murder's clothes. The room is the puzzle; the crime is the decoration.

Key points:
- Exhaust every entrance and mechanism.
- Classic solutions form a known catalog.
- Fair play: the mechanism must be clued.
- The room is the puzzle.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Sealed Study

900141.title: The Locked Cabin
900141.description: Isolation as a locked room: the snowbound impossible.
900141.content:
The Locked Cabin — Isolation as a locked room: the snowbound impossible.

The locked cabin moves the impossible crime to the wilderness: a cabin in deep snow, no footprints but the victim's, the door barred from inside. The snow is the perfect locked room — it records every approach, and its blankness is the testimony. The solution space is the snow trick catalog: the approach over the roof, the footprints brushed away, the path that was never needed. The atmosphere does half the work: isolation raises the stakes and shrinks the suspect list to the people in the cabin. The locked cabin's lesson for puzzle designers is that the environment can be the lock. The snow remembers everything — except what it was made to forget.

Key points:
- Snow records every approach.
- The solution space is the snow-trick catalog.
- Isolation shrinks the suspect list.
- The environment can be the lock.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Locked Cabin

900142.title: The Impossible Disappearance
900142.description: The reverse locked room: someone vanishes from a sealed space.
900142.content:
The Impossible Disappearance — The reverse locked room: someone vanishes from a sealed space.

The impossible disappearance inverts the locked room: instead of a crime in a sealed space, a person vanishes from one — the guarded room, the watched corridor, the empty stage. The puzzle's engine is the continuity audit: the solver must verify that the surveillance was truly continuous, because every disappearance solution hides a gap. The classic gaps are the changed clothes, the hidden compartment in the crowd, the moment everyone looked away at once. The designer's craft is the timeline: lay out every minute so the solver can find the seam. The disappearance's thrill is existential — a person cannot vanish, so the world must be lying about something. Find the lie and you find the person.

Key points:
- Audit the surveillance for gaps.
- Every vanishing hides a seam in time.
- Lay out the timeline completely.
- The world is lying about something.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Impossible Disappearance

900143.title: The Snowbound Alibi
900143.description: No one could have come or gone: the alibi as locked room.
900143.content:
The Snowbound Alibi — No one could have come or gone: the alibi as locked room.

The snowbound alibi turns the locked room inside out: the question isn't how the crime was done in a sealed room, but how anyone could have been there at all. The snow's testimony — no tracks in, no tracks out — makes every suspect's presence impossible. The solution catalog is the presence trick: the suspect never left (hidden in the scene), never arrived (the crime was timed), or the snow itself lied (wind, melt, the covered path). The puzzle's beauty is the double lock: the room is sealed AND the approach is impossible. The snowbound alibi teaches that impossibility compounds — two locks need two keys, and the solver must find both. The snow is the witness; cross-examine it.

Key points:
- Double lock: sealed room plus impossible approach.
- Presence tricks: hidden, timed, or snow-lied.
- Two locks need two keys.
- Cross-examine the snow.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Snowbound Alibi

900144.title: The Locked Room Writer's Toolkit
900144.description: The craft kit: mechanisms, misdirection, and fair play.
900144.content:
The Locked Room Writer's Toolkit — The craft kit: mechanisms, misdirection, and fair play.

The locked-room writer's toolkit has three drawers: mechanisms (the catalog of physical tricks), misdirection (the art of pointing at the wrong lock), and fair play (the contract with the reader). The mechanism drawer holds the classics — thread, wire, gravity, timing — each with known clue requirements. The misdirection drawer holds the narrative tools: the emphasized irrelevant detail, the buried crucial one, the suspect who absorbs suspicion. The fair-play drawer holds the rules: the reader must have every fact the detective has, and the solution must be the best explanation of the clues. The toolkit's master rule is that the trick must be simple — the best locked rooms have solutions a child could understand and an adult would never guess. Simple trick; deep puzzle.

Key points:
- Three drawers: mechanism, misdirection, fair play.
- The reader gets every fact the detective has.
- The solution must be the best explanation.
- Simple trick; deep puzzle.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Locked Room Writer's Toolkit

900145.title: The Mechanical Trick Catalog
900145.description: Every physical way to fake a sealed room.
900145.content:
The Mechanical Trick Catalog — Every physical way to fake a sealed room.

The mechanical trick catalog is the locked room's engineering reference: every known way to make a room look sealed. The bolt tricks (thread through the keyhole, the falling bar), the window tricks (the latch that catches on closing, the pane removed and replaced), the key tricks (the key turned from outside with pliers and wire, the duplicate left inside). The door tricks (the panel that swings both ways, the hinges lifted), and the timing tricks (the lock engaged after the crime by a delayed mechanism). The catalog's use is twofold: writers pick tricks to build puzzles, and solvers study tricks to break them. The catalog's warning is staleness — the famous tricks are known, so the modern writer must combine or invert them. The physics hasn't changed; the combinations are infinite.

Key points:
- Bolt, window, key, door, and timing tricks.
- Writers build from it; solvers break with it.
- Famous tricks need fresh combinations.
- The combinations are infinite.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Mechanical Trick Catalog

900146.title: The Psychological Lock
900146.description: No bars, no bolts: the room sealed by the mind.
900146.content:
The Psychological Lock — No bars, no bolts: the room sealed by the mind.

The psychological lock is the locked room's subtlest form: the room wasn't physically sealed — it was sealed by belief, habit, or fear. The classic is the door everyone assumed was locked, the corridor no one would walk at night, the room the staff never enter. The puzzle's engine is assumption audit: the solver must question what the narrative asserted without proving. The design craft is the planted assumption — a single line early on ('the door was always kept locked') that the reader accepts and never verifies. The reveal reframes everything: the impossible crime was merely an unexamined premise. The psychological lock teaches the deepest puzzle lesson: the strongest locks are the ones we install in our own thinking. Question the given.

Key points:
- Sealed by belief, not by bars.
- Audit every unexamined assumption.
- Plant the premise early and quietly.
- The strongest locks are mental.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Psychological Lock

900147.title: The Timed Lock Puzzle
900147.description: The crime happened when no one could: the alibi machine.
900147.content:
The Timed Lock Puzzle — The crime happened when no one could: the alibi machine.

The timed lock puzzle makes time itself the sealed room: the crime occurred in a window when every suspect has an ironclad alibi. The mechanism is the alibi machine — the timed device, the delayed action, the crime set in motion hours before it happens. The classic forms are the ice-melt trigger, the slow poison, the recorded sound that fakes a time of death. The solver's tool is the timeline: lay every alibi against every minute and find the overlap that isn't. The designer's discipline is the clockwork's fairness — the timing mechanism must be deducible from the scene's physical facts. The timed lock's thrill is the long fuse: the criminal left hours ago, and time did the deed. The clock is the accomplice.

Key points:
- Time is the sealed room.
- The timeline is the solver's tool.
- Timing mechanisms must be deducible.
- The clock is the accomplice.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Timed Lock Puzzle

900148.title: Fair Play: Cluing the Impossible
900148.description: The contract: every clue the solution needs, on the page.
900148.content:
Fair Play: Cluing the Impossible — The contract: every clue the solution needs, on the page.

Fair play is the locked room's sacred contract: the reader must have access to every clue the solution requires, fairly presented before the reveal. The craft is the clue hierarchy — the crucial facts stated plainly but quietly, surrounded by louder irrelevancies, so the solver could have seen it. The techniques are the emphasized trivial (a long paragraph about the curtains), the buried crucial (the lock's brand in a list), and the misread plain (the clue stated so simply it's dismissed). The violation is the smuggled fact: the detective knew something the reader never saw. The fair-play test is the reread: after the reveal, the reader should see the solution shining in the early chapters. The game is only fun if it can be won. Clue honestly.

Key points:
- Every needed clue on the page, pre-reveal.
- Hierarchy: quiet crucial, loud irrelevant.
- The reread test proves fairness.
- The game must be winnable.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - Fair Play: Cluing the Impossible

900149.title: The Locked Room Canon
900149.description: The hundred-year lineage: from Poe to the present.
900149.content:
The Locked Room Canon — The hundred-year lineage: from Poe to the present.

The locked-room canon runs from Poe's Rue Morgue in 1841 through the golden age masters to the modern revival, and its lineage is a curriculum in impossible-crime design. The landmarks are the founding trick (Poe's window), the encyclopedic catalogs (Carr's locked-room lectures), and the modern inversions that play fair with readers who know the classics. The canon's study value is pattern recognition: read twenty locked rooms and the trick families reveal themselves, which is exactly what the modern writer must defeat. The canon's living edge is the global revival — Japanese shin honkaku and its heirs treat the locked room as pure logic art. The canon is not a museum; it's a toolbox with a hundred years of edge. Study the lineage; then pick the lock.

Key points:
- Poe to the golden age to the modern revival.
- Study landmarks: window, lectures, inversions.
- Pattern recognition is the canon's gift.
- The canon is a toolbox, not a museum.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Locked Room Canon

900150.title: The Cryptex, Explained
900150.content:
The Cryptex, Explained — Anatomy of the letter-lock cylinder.

The cryptex is five rings of letters on a cylinder, and its anatomy is the gated channel: inside, a pin rides in a track that only opens when every ring's gate aligns. The solver's experience is pure combination space — with 26 letters on 5 rings, brute force is 11 million tries, so the puzzle must be solved by wit, not stamina. The maker's craft is the gate cutting: each ring's internal notch must align at exactly one rotation, with tolerances that forgive the hand but not the guess. The collector's note is that most cryptexes on the market are decorative — a working one has a satisfying mechanical honesty you can feel. The cryptex is a combination lock that went to theater school. The word is the key.

Key points:
- Gated channels make the letter-lock.
- Brute force is 11 million tries: solve by wit.
- Gate tolerances forgive hands, not guesses.
- Working cryptexes feel mechanically honest.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Cryptex, Explained

900151.title: Puzzle Padlocks
900151.description: A lock that opens for cleverness, not keys.
900151.content:
Puzzle Padlocks — A lock that opens for cleverness, not keys.

The puzzle padlock looks like security hardware and behaves like a riddle: the shackle releases only when the solver finds the hidden move — the sliding plate, the rotated dial, the magnetic catch. The family splits into keyless trick locks (no key exists; the mechanism is the puzzle) and keyed puzzles (the key is hidden in the lock's own body). The design principle is the honest fake: it must look like a real lock to set expectations, then violate them delightfully. The solver's toolkit is manipulation — feel for gates, listen for clicks, map the moving parts by touch. The puzzle padlock's charm is the category error: you brought lockpicking skills to a puzzle fight. The key was never the answer.

Key points:
- Trick locks have no key; the mechanism is the puzzle.
- Look like a lock; behave like a riddle.
- Solve by feel: gates, clicks, moving parts.
- The key was never the answer.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - Puzzle Padlocks

900152.title: The Torture Cube: Burr Puzzles
900152.description: Six notched sticks, one impossible assembly.
900152.content:
The Torture Cube: Burr Puzzles — Six notched sticks, one impossible assembly.

The burr puzzle — six notched sticks interlocked into a cube — is the puzzle gadget's endurance event: it assembles in exactly one sequence, and every wrong path jams. The mathematics is the notch combinatorics: each stick's notches must clear the others in a precise order, and the classic six-piece burr has a unique assembly sequence. The solver's discipline is the systematic search — try, backtrack, record — because random fiddling never converges. The maker's craft is the notch fitting: too tight and the puzzle is a paperweight, too loose and it falls apart in the hand. The burr's lesson is humility: six sticks, no moving parts, and hours of defeat. Simplicity is the cruelest complexity.

Key points:
- Unique assembly sequence; wrong paths jam.
- Systematic search beats random fiddling.
- Notch fit decides solvability.
- Six sticks, hours of defeat.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Torture Cube: Burr Puzzles

900153.title: The Secret Compartment Ring
900153.description: Jewelry with a hiding place: the ring's tiny vault.
900153.content:
The Secret Compartment Ring — Jewelry with a hiding place: the ring's tiny vault.

The secret compartment ring hides a vault in a band of metal: a hinged bezel, a sliding panel, or a threaded cap concealing a space for a note, a pill, or a keepsake. The engineering is miniaturization — the hinge must be invisible at arm's length, the catch must survive daily wear, and the whole thing must still be a wearable ring. The history is the poison ring's respectable descendant: the same mechanism, redeemed for love notes and emergency pills. The maker's challenge is the tolerance at small scale: a tenth of a millimeter is a canyon at ring scale. The ring's romance is the secret worn openly — the most intimate puzzle is the one you never take off. Hidden in plain sight, on the hand.

Key points:
- Hinge invisible at arm's length.
- Catch must survive daily wear.
- Tolerances are canyons at ring scale.
- The secret worn openly.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Secret Compartment Ring

900154.title: The Labyrinth Flask
900154.description: A maze you drink from: the puzzle decanter.
900154.content:
The Labyrinth Flask — A maze you drink from: the puzzle decanter.

The labyrinth flask is a decanter with a maze built into the pour: tilt it wrong and nothing comes out; find the path and the drink flows. The mechanism is internal baffling — walls inside the vessel that channel liquid along exactly one route to the spout. The design is the pour path: the maker must ensure the maze is solvable by feel and tilt, since the solver can't see inside. The party value is enormous — the flask turns serving drinks into a performance. The engineering constraint is cleaning: the baffles must not trap residue, so the design favors smooth channels over sharp traps. The labyrinth flask proves that puzzles can be hospitality. The drink is the prize; the maze is the toast.

Key points:
- Internal baffles channel the pour.
- Solvable by feel and tilt alone.
- Design for cleaning: smooth channels.
- Puzzles can be hospitality.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Labyrinth Flask

900155.title: The Stubborn Matchbox
900155.description: A matchbox that refuses to open normally.
900155.content:
The Stubborn Matchbox — A matchbox that refuses to open normally.

The trick matchbox looks like an ordinary matchbox and opens like nothing you've handled: the drawer slides only after a press, a tilt, or a sequence the box demands. The mechanism is the standard matchbox drawer plus one secret — a catch, a false panel, or a reversed slide — which is enough to defeat every habitual motion. The design genius is the familiar form: the solver's hands know matchboxes, and the box exploits that knowledge. The maker's build is a modification project — start with a real matchbox, add the secret, refinish so the tampering vanishes. The trick matchbox's lesson is about habit: the strongest lock on a familiar object is the user's own muscle memory. The hands must unlearn.

Key points:
- One secret added to a familiar form.
- Exploit the solver's muscle memory.
- Build by modifying a real matchbox.
- Habit is the lock.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Stubborn Matchbox

900156.title: The Puzzle Wallet
900156.description: Your cards, guarded by a sequence.
900156.content:
The Puzzle Wallet — Your cards, guarded by a sequence.

The puzzle wallet keeps cards behind a mechanical sequence: panels slide, flaps fold, and the money emerges only for the initiated. The engineering is flat-pack kinematics — every motion must work in two dimensions, since a wallet can't be thick. The materials are the challenge: leather stretches, so the puzzle elements are usually metal or rigid inlays within the leather shell. The daily-use test is brutal — a puzzle wallet that takes a minute to open gets abandoned, so the sequence must be quick for the owner and opaque to the thief. The wallet's philosophy is security through obscurity done right: not a lock, but a ritual. The owner knows the dance; the pickpocket doesn't.

Key points:
- Flat-pack kinematics: thin mechanisms.
- Rigid puzzle inlays in a leather shell.
- Fast for the owner, opaque to the thief.
- Security as ritual, not lock.

demo.title: Interactive record tour - The Puzzle Wallet

900157.title: The Entangled Nails
900157.content:
The Entangled Nails — Two nails, one impossible embrace.

The entangled nails are the puzzle gadget's minimal poem: two bent nails hooked together, separable only by the one true motion. The topology is the puzzle — the nails' bends create a linked state with exactly one unlinked path, and every wrong move tightens the embrace. The solver's method is the motion map: explore the degrees of freedom systematically — rotate, slide, tilt — until the path reveals itself. The maker's craft is the bend: the curves must be smooth enough to slide and sharp enough to catch, a balance struck by hand and tested by solving. The nails' lesson is topological: the answer was never force, it was geometry. Two nails, one path, zero force.

Key points:
- Topology is the puzzle.
- Map motions systematically: rotate, slide, tilt.

900158.title: The Gadget Collector's Guide
900158.description: Building a collection: curation, care, and the hunt.
900158.content:
The Gadget Collector's Guide — Building a collection: curation, care, and the hunt.

The puzzle gadget collection is a museum of ingenuity: the collector's craft is curation — choosing pieces that represent mechanisms, eras, and makers, not just accumulating shiny objects. The acquisition channels are the hunt's joy: puzzle swaps, maker direct, estate sales, and the annual gatherings where the rarest pieces change hands. The documentation discipline separates collectors from hoarders: photograph each piece, record its maker and mechanism, note its solution (sealed, for the next owner). The care rules are mechanical — oil the moving parts, control humidity, never force a stuck antique. The collection's purpose is the demonstration: a great collection is a library you can hand to a guest. Collect to share.

Key points:
- Curate mechanisms, eras, makers — not shiny objects.
- Document: photo, maker, mechanism, sealed solution.
- Oil moving parts; control humidity.
- A collection is a library to hand guests.

900159.title: Caring for Mechanical Puzzles
900159.description: Maintenance for a lifetime of solving.
900159.content:
Caring for Mechanical Puzzles — Maintenance for a lifetime of solving.

Mechanical puzzles are machines, and machines need maintenance: the care routine is cleaning, lubrication, and inspection on a schedule the collection's size determines. The cleaning rule is dry first — brushes and air before any solvent, because wood and solvent are old enemies. The lubrication doctrine is minimal and correct: a whisper of wax on wooden slides, a drop of fine oil on metal pivots, never WD-40 on anything you love. The inspection habit catches the wear before the failure: check cords, springs, and catches annually. The storage rules are environmental — stable humidity, no attics, no basements. The maintained puzzle solves like new for decades. Care is the other half of the craft.

Key points:
- Clean dry first; solvents last.
- Minimal correct lubrication only.
- Inspect cords, springs, catches annually.
- Stable humidity; no attics or basements.

900160.title: The Nonogram Loom
900160.description: Weaving pictures from numbers: the nonogram generator.
900160.content:
The Nonogram Loom — Weaving pictures from numbers: the nonogram generator.

The nonogram loom weaves pictures from numbers: the generator starts with a pixel image, computes the row and column run-lengths, and the puzzle is the reverse — reconstruct the image from the numbers alone. The generation craft is the image selection: bold silhouettes with clean runs make fair puzzles; noisy photos make impossible ones. The solvability guarantee is the logic check — the generator must verify the puzzle has a unique solution by logic alone, no guessing, which means simulating a solver. The difficulty dial is the image complexity: 10x10 icons for beginners, 30x30 scenes for the devoted. The loom's product is the magic moment when numbers become a picture. The grid is the loom; the numbers are the thread.

Key points:
- Generate from bold silhouette images.
- Verify unique solution by logic alone.
- Scale difficulty with grid size.
- Numbers become pictures.

900161.title: The Kakuro Kiln
900161.description: Firing up cross-sums: the kakuro generator.
900161.content:
The Kakuro Kiln — Firing up cross-sums: the kakuro generator.

The kakuro kiln fires up cross-sums: the generator places sum clues on a grid and fills it with digits that satisfy every clue, no repeats in any run. The generation algorithm is constraint propagation — fill cells, propagate the sum constraints, backtrack on conflict — the same engine that solves, run in reverse. The quality control is the uniqueness proof: the kiln must confirm exactly one solution, because a kakuro with two solutions is a broken promise. The difficulty levers are grid density and clue generosity: sparse clues and long runs for experts, generous clues and short runs for learners. The kiln's output is the crossword of arithmetic. The sums are the clay; the digits are the fire.

Key points:
- Constraint propagation, run in reverse.
- Prove solution uniqueness.
- Tune with clue generosity and run length.
- The crossword of arithmetic.

900162.title: The Slitherlink Press
900162.content:
The Slitherlink Press — Stamping loops: the slitherlink generator.

The slitherlink press stamps out loop puzzles: the generator draws a random single loop on a dot grid, writes the adjacency numbers, and erases the loop — the solver's job is to redraw it. The generation subtlety is the loop drawing: the random loop must be interesting, with a mix of straight runs and turns, not a boring rectangle. The solvability engine is the logic simulator: the press verifies the puzzle yields to deduction alone, applying the standard slitherlink theorems. The difficulty dial is the given density: more numbers for beginners, sparser clues for veterans. The press's signature is the single-loop guarantee — the solver always knows there's exactly one loop. One loop; infinite variety.

Key points:
- Draw interesting random loops.
- Verify solvability by logic simulation.
- Tune with clue density.
- The single-loop guarantee.

900163.title: The KenKen Assembly Line
900163.description: Cages and arithmetic: the KenKen factory.
900163.content:
The KenKen Assembly Line — Cages and arithmetic: the KenKen factory.

The KenKen assembly line builds arithmetic cages: the generator partitions the grid into cages, assigns each a target and operation, and fills the grid with a Latin square underneath. The generation order matters — fill the Latin square first, then carve cages around it, so the solution is guaranteed from the start. The cage design is the craft: cage shapes must be contiguous, targets must be achievable, and the operation set should mix —, +, ×, ÷ for variety. The difficulty levers are grid size and cage generosity: 4x4 with small cages for learners, 9x9 with sprawling cages for the brave. The assembly line's promise is the clean cage: every puzzle solvable, every solution unique. Arithmetic, caged.

Key points:
- Latin square first, cages second.
- Contiguous cages, achievable targets.
- Mix operations for variety.
- Every puzzle solvable, uniquely.

900164.title: The Acrostic Engine
900164.description: Quotes into puzzles: the acrostic generator.
900164.content:
The Acrostic Engine — Quotes into puzzles: the acrostic generator.

The acrostic engine turns quotations into puzzles: take a quote, split it into words, clue each word, and the initial letters spell the author. The generation pipeline is quote selection (pithy, attributed, splittable), word clueing (definitions or cryptic hints), and letter mapping (initials spell the source). The quality bar is the quote: it must be worth the work — the solver's reward for the long solve is a line worth remembering. The clue craft is the difficulty dial: straightforward definitions for casual solvers, cryptic wordplay for the initiated. The engine's signature is the double payoff: solve the words, then read the quote, then name the author. Three puzzles in one. The quote is the treasure.

Key points:
- Pick quotes worth the effort.
- Clue words straight or cryptic.
- Initials spell the author.
- Triple payoff: words, quote, author.

900165.title: The Cryptic Clue Mill
900165.description: Grinding wordplay: the cryptic generator's art.
900165.content:
The Cryptic Clue Mill — Grinding wordplay: the cryptic generator's art.

The cryptic clue mill grinds out wordplay: the generator takes an answer word and builds a clue with definition plus wordplay — anagram, container, hidden, homophone. The generation is the hard part of cryptics: the mill needs word lists with letter-pattern indexes, so it can find fodder for anagrams and containers mechanically. The quality control is the surface reading: the clue must read as a plausible sentence while secretly encoding the answer, and the mill's output needs human polishing. The fairness rules are the cryptic contract: the definition must be exact, the wordplay must be sound, the indicator words must be honest. The mill's product is the penny-drop: the solver sees the trick and the answer together. Wordplay, engineered.

Key points:
- Definition plus sound wordplay.
- Letter-pattern indexes find fodder.
- Surface readings need human polish.
- The contract: exact, sound, honest.

900166.title: The Domino Tiling Shop
900166.description: Covering boards with dominoes: the tiling generator.
900166.content:
The Domino Tiling Shop — Covering boards with dominoes: the tiling generator.

The domino tiling shop covers boards with 2x1 rectangles: the generator punches holes or colors in a pattern, and the puzzle is to tile the rest — or prove it can't be done. The generation craft is the mutilated board: remove two same-color squares from a chessboard and the tiling is impossible, a parity argument the solver must discover. The difficulty dial is the subtlety of the invariant: color parity for beginners, more exotic invariants (modular colorings) for experts. The shop's teaching value is proof: tiling puzzles are most solvers' first encounter with impossibility arguments. The product is the elegant no: sometimes the answer is a proof, not a tiling. Cover the board — or prove you can't.

Key points:
- Mutilated boards teach parity.
- Invariants scale the difficulty.
- Tiling puzzles teach impossibility proofs.
- Sometimes the answer is a proof.

900167.title: The Pentomino Packery
900167.description: Twelve pieces, endless boxes: the pentomino packer.
900167.content:
The Pentomino Packery — Twelve pieces, endless boxes: the pentomino packer.

The pentomino packery packs twelve pieces into rectangles: the generator picks a target rectangle (6x10, 5x12, 4x15, 3x20) and the puzzle is the packing. The generation is the solution harvest: the packery's solver finds packings, and the puzzle is the rectangle with the solution hidden. The difficulty truth is that all rectangles are hard — the 6x10 has 2,339 solutions but finding one by hand is still a journey. The variant dial is the hole: punch one square out and the puzzle becomes a placement-plus-packing hybrid. The packery's charm is the physicality: pentominoes beg to be handled, and the workshop keeps a wooden set on the bench. Twelve pieces; four rectangles; infinite afternoons.

Key points:
- Harvest solutions with a solver.
- All rectangles are hard by hand.
- Hole variants add placement puzzles.
- Pentominoes beg to be handled.

900168.title: The Puzzle Zine Press
900168.description: From generator to newsprint: publishing puzzle collections.
900168.content:
The Puzzle Zine Press — From generator to newsprint: publishing puzzle collections.

The puzzle zine press turns generator output into a printed zine: curate a set, lay it out, print it, staple it, and the infinite workshop becomes a physical object. The curation is the craft: a good zine has an arc — easy openers, a meaty middle, a showpiece closer — not a random pile. The layout rules are print-specific: generous white space, solution sections that don't spoil adjacent puzzles, and a difficulty key on the contents page. The distribution is the community: leave zines at cafes, trade at meetups, mail to subscribers. The press's lesson is that the generator's infinite output gains value from finite curation. Infinity is the raw material; the zine is the product. Print the infinite.

Key points:
- Curate an arc: opener, middle, closer.
- Layout must not spoil adjacent puzzles.
- Distribute through community channels.
- Finite curation gives infinity value.

900169.title: The Infinite Arcade Cabinet
900169.description: The workshop's front door: a cabinet that never repeats.
900169.content:
The Infinite Arcade Cabinet — The workshop's front door: a cabinet that never repeats.

The infinite arcade cabinet is the workshop's front door: a kiosk that serves a fresh puzzle every visit, generated on the spot, never repeating. The build is a small computer, a touchscreen, and the generator suite — the cabinet is the showroom for everything the workshop makes. The UX is the craft: one tap for a new puzzle, difficulty that adapts to the player's history, and a print button for the paper loyalists. The placement strategy is the business: cafes, libraries, waiting rooms — anywhere people have idle minutes and itchy brains. The cabinet's magic is the endless new: the regular who plays daily never sees the same puzzle twice. The workshop's output, one tap at a time. Never the same puzzle twice.

- Fresh puzzle every visit, generated live.
- Adaptive difficulty from player history.
- Place where idle minutes live.
- The endless new keeps regulars.

JAH-PUZZLE-000117.title: The Sprint Solve Format
JAH-PUZZLE-000117.description: One puzzle, one clock, one winner: the anatomy of a sprint.
JAH-PUZZLE-000117.content:
The Sprint Solve Format — One puzzle, one clock, one winner: the anatomy of a sprint.

The sprint is the purest race in puzzling: every solver gets the identical puzzle and the clock decides. The format works because it isolates solving skill from puzzle choice — no one can blame the draw. The classic sprint is the crossword dash: fifteen minutes, one grid, the fastest clean solve wins, with penalties for wrong squares. The organizer's duties are few but absolute: identical puzzles, synchronized starts, and a judging standard published before the first pencil moves. The sprint's drama is compression — an hour of thinking collapsed into minutes of visible racing. Run one and watch quiet solvers become athletes.

Key points:
- Identical puzzles for every solver.
- Synchronized starts; published judging rules.
- Penalties for errors keep speed honest.
- Compression is the drama.
